lead: An operating system must defend itself against people who mean harm, not only against programs that make mistakes. Protection asks whether a process may read this file; security asks who is on the network and what they are trying. Authentication, authorisation, isolation and audit form a chain that is only as strong as its weakest link. You meet the chain daily: a UPI PIN, an OTP on your phone, a bank firewall that opens only port 443. This chapter names the common threats and the standard defences, without going inside the algorithms.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for the split between protection and security, and Unit 1, OS operations: dual mode and timers, for the hardware support every defence leans on.

sections.h3: Security is about a person, not a bug

blocks.text: Protection is internal and mechanical: it decides whether a process may read a file, using the access matrix of 6.3. Security asks a harder question: is a person deliberately making the system act against its owner? A faulty program makes accidents. An attacker makes plans, studies your system, and changes method when one fails.

Three goals appear in every paper. Confidentiality: data is read only by parties allowed to read it. Integrity: data is changed only in allowed ways. Availability: the service keeps answering. A denial of service attacks availability alone and never touches a byte of data.

Keep the words apart. An asset is what you protect: account data, a database, a key. A vulnerability is a weakness in design or code. A threat is a potential violation of security that could cause harm. The threat agent, or attacker, is the person or group who may carry it out. An attack is the attempt. The attack surface is everything an outsider can reach: open ports, web forms, email, USB ports, even the help-desk phone number.

Every defence rests on four pillars: authentication (who are you), authorisation (what may you do), isolation (how far can damage spread), and audit (what can we prove afterwards). The chain is only as strong as its weakest link. A 12-character password gains nothing if the server still accepts the default administrator login.
Program threats arrive inside software you install or input you send. The standard list:

items: Trojan horse: looks useful, carries hidden harmful code. A free video converter that also opens a back door.
Trap door (backdoor): a secret entry left by the writer that skips normal authentication. One line in the login code is enough.
Logic bomb: dormant code that fires on a condition, such as a payroll script that wipes files when a dismissed employee's name disappears.
Virus: a fragment that copies itself into a host file or boot sector and runs when the host runs. It needs a host, and usually a user action.
Worm: a standalone program that spreads by itself over the network through a listening service. No host file, no user action.
Ransomware: encrypts files and demands money for the key; the carrier is often a trojan or a worm.

Buffer overflow: a program writes more bytes than a buffer holds. On the call stack the extra bytes overwrite the return address, so a crafted input makes the CPU jump into attacker code. Defences: bounds checks, a non-executable stack, address randomisation.

sections.h3: Network threats, and cryptography as a tool

blocks.text: Network threats arrive through the ports your machine is listening on.

items: Port scan: connect to many ports to learn which services answer. This is reconnaissance, not the break-in.
Denial of service (DoS): flood one service until real users cannot get in. A distributed denial of service (DDoS) uses thousands of hijacked machines, a botnet.
Spoofing: forging a source IP address, or an email sender name, so traffic looks like it came from a trusted party.
Man-in-the-middle: the attacker sits on the path between two parties, relays their traffic and reads or alters it.

blocks.text: Cryptography is the toolbox that makes the last two hard.

items: Symmetric key: one secret key both encrypts and decrypts. Fast; delivering the key is the hard part.
Public key: a public key encrypts and only the matching private key decrypts. Solves delivery; slow.
Hash: a fixed-length fingerprint of data, easy to compute and infeasible to invert. Used for integrity checks and password storage.
Digital signature: a hash of the message encrypted with the sender's private key. Proves origin and integrity, and the sender cannot deny it.
TLS: uses public key methods once to agree a symmetric session key, then symmetric encryption for the data. It is the padlock in the browser.

blocks.text: User authentication uses three kinds of evidence: something you know (password, PIN), something you have (OTP on a phone, hardware token), something you are (fingerprint, iris). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines two different kinds; two passwords are not MFA.
Passwords are stored as a salted hash, never as text. Their strength is the size of the search space.

blocks.where: N is the number of possible passwords; A is the alphabet size in characters (26 for lowercase letters, 62 with capitals and digits); L is the length in characters. An attacker who knows nothing about the user needs N ÷ 2 guesses on average.

blocks.text: Defences sit inside the operating system and around it.

items: Firewall: rules that drop or pass packets by address and port, as in the figure.
Patching: closing the vulnerability the attacker already knows about.
Sandbox: run untrusted code in a restricted domain so damage is contained; the domain idea of 6.2 applied to apps.
Least privilege: give each process and user the smallest set of rights it needs; a capability from 6.5 carries them.
Audit logs: a record of logins, failures and file access, so an incident can be reconstructed.

blocks.text: Evaluation classes rise in assurance: D minimal protection; C1 discretionary protection with separate users; C2 controlled access with auditing; B1 labelled security; B2 structured protection; B3 security domains; A1 formally verified design. One line each is enough for an exam.

examples.question: A password is 8 characters long. Case 1 uses only the 26 lowercase letters. Case 2 uses 62 characters (a-z, A-Z, 0-9). The attacker's tool tests 10⁹ guesses per second. Find the number of possible passwords, the average number of guesses and the average search time in each case, and the gain from widening the alphabet.
steps: Case 1: alphabet A = 26, length L = 8. Password space N = A^L = 26⁸ = 208,827,064,576, about 2.09 × 10¹¹.
The right password is equally likely to sit anywhere in the list, so the average is half the space: 208,827,064,576 ÷ 2 = 104,413,532,288 guesses.
Time = guesses ÷ rate = 104,413,532,288 ÷ 10⁹ = 104.4 s, under two minutes.
In hours: 109,170.1 ÷ 3600 = 30.3 hours, about one and a quarter days.
Gain at the same length = 62⁸ ÷ 26⁸ = 2.18 × 10¹⁴ ÷ 2.09 × 10¹¹ = 1045.5, roughly a factor of 1000. Length and alphabet both count.
examples.answer: Case 1 falls in 104.4 s (about 2 minutes); case 2 needs 109,170.1 s, that is 30.3 hours, a gain of 1046 times from the wider alphabet.
examples.check:
rate = 1e9
p1 = 26**8
p2 = 62**8
print(p1)
print(p1 // 2)
print(round(p1 / 2 / rate, 1))
print(p2)
print(p2 // 2)
print(round(p2 / 2 / rate, 1))
print(round(p2 / 2 / rate / 3600, 1))
print(round(p2 / p1))

traps: Virus and worm are not the same. A virus needs a host file and usually a user action; a worm spreads by itself over the network.
A port scan is reconnaissance, not a break-in. Writing that the scan deleted data loses marks.
Denial of service attacks availability only. It does not read or change data, so do not claim a confidentiality loss.
Cryptography alone is not security. A perfectly encrypted channel to an unpatched server is still broken, and a digital signature gives origin and integrity, not secrecy.
Authentication is not authorisation. Proving who you are does not decide what you may do, and the examiner tests exactly this line.

quiz.q: Define a trojan horse and a trap door, one line each.
quiz.a: A trojan horse is a program that looks useful but carries hidden harmful code. A trap door is a secret entry point left in the code that skips normal authentication.

quiz.q: Why does a worm spread without user action while a virus usually needs one?
quiz.a: A worm is a standalone program that reaches other machines over the network through a listening service. A virus is code inside a host file and runs only when the host is executed, so opening the file is what triggers it.

quiz.q: A 4-digit PIN uses digits 0-9. The attacker tests 10³ PINs per second. Find the average time to find the PIN.
A system has user accounts, an access list per file, and logs every login. Which evaluation class fits, and why?
quiz.a: C2, controlled access protection: access is controlled per user through lists and the system keeps audit records of logins.

quiz.q: A firewall allows only port 443. Explain why the web application behind it can still be broken into.
quiz.a: A firewall filters addresses and ports, not content. A crafted request on port 443 reaches the web service and exploits its own bugs, such as a buffer overflow or a missing authorisation check. The defence must continue inside the service: patching, input checks, least privilege.

quiz.q: A service uses an 8-character password plus an OTP. Explain the claim that the chain is as strong as its weakest link.
quiz.a: The OTP stops reuse of a stolen password. But if the reset desk hands a new password to anyone who knows a date of birth, the attacker bypasses both factors. Strength is set by the weakest step, not by the best one, so the reset procedure must be audited and checked as carefully as the login.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry has moved from trusting everything inside the office network to zero trust, where every request is authenticated and authorised again, because remote work and cloud servers erased the inside. Supply-chain attacks, where the attacker poisons a library or an update server, are now a leading cause of breaches. Hardware roots of trust such as TPM chips and secure boot push the first check below the operating system. Search for zero trust architecture, secure boot, and fuzzing for the testing side.
